reference_title: Eurocode 7: Geotechnical Design - Part 1: General Rules

sections.title: General
sections.summary: Requires careful collection, recording, and interpretation of geotechnical information (geology, geomorphology, seismicity, hydrology, site history), with investigations planned to the construction/performance requirements and continuously reviewed as new information is obtained; routine field/lab testing follows recognised standards (EN 1997-2).
sections.body: Careful collection, recording and interpretation of geotechnical information shall always be made, including geology, geomorphology, seismicity, hydrology, and the history of the site; indications of the variability of the ground shall be taken into account. Geotechnical investigations shall be planned taking into account the construction and performance requirements of the proposed structure, and their scope shall be continuously reviewed as new information is obtained during execution of the work. Routine field investigations and laboratory testing shall be carried out and reported generally in accordance with internationally recognised standards and recommendations (see EN 1997-2); deviations from these standards and additional test requirements shall be reported.
key_points: Geotechnical information must include geology, geomorphology, seismicity, hydrology, and site history
Investigation scope is planned to construction/performance needs and continuously reviewed as work proceeds
Field/lab testing follows internationally recognised standards; EN 1997-2 gives detailed requirements
Deviations from standard procedures and any additional test requirements must be reported
sections.applicability: General principles governing the collection and use of geotechnical data for any geotechnical design.

sections.title: Geotechnical investigations - General
sections.summary: Geotechnical investigations must provide sufficient data on the ground and ground-water conditions for a reliable assessment of characteristic parameter values; investigation scope is matched to the investigation phase and Geotechnical Category (EN 1997-2, Section 2), and should include site visual inspection.
sections.body: Geotechnical investigations shall provide sufficient data concerning the ground and the ground-water conditions at and around the construction site for a proper description of the essential ground properties and a reliable assessment of the characteristic values of the ground parameters used in design calculations. The composition and amount of investigation shall be adjusted to the particular investigation phase and the Geotechnical Category (see EN 1997-2, Section 2). For very large or unusual structures, structures with abnormal risks or difficult ground/loading conditions, and structures in highly seismic areas, the extent of investigation specified in EN 1997 may not be sufficient. Ground conditions influencing the choice of Geotechnical Category should be determined as early as possible, and investigations should include a visual site inspection to allow later verification of design assumptions.
key_points: Investigations must reliably support characteristic values of ground parameters
Investigation scope scales with investigation phase and Geotechnical Category (EN 1997-2 Section 2)
Very large/unusual/high-risk/highly-seismic structures may need investigation beyond the EN 1997 minimum
Site visual inspection should be included to allow design assumptions to be verified during construction
sections.applicability: Governs the scope and depth of geotechnical site investigation programmes.

sections.title: Preliminary investigations
sections.summary: Preliminary investigations assess general site suitability, compare alternative sites, estimate changes caused by the works, plan design/control investigations (including the extent of ground with significant influence on structure behaviour), and identify borrow areas.
sections.body: Preliminary investigations shall be carried out to assess the general suitability of the site, to compare alternative sites where relevant, to estimate the changes that may be caused by the proposed works, to plan the design and control investigations (including identifying the extent of ground that may significantly influence structure behaviour), and to identify borrow areas where relevant.
key_points: Assesses general site suitability and compares alternative sites
Estimates changes the proposed works may cause to the site
Plans the subsequent design and control investigation phases
Identifies borrow areas where relevant
sections.applicability: Early-phase site investigation, typically pre-design, to inform siting and later investigation planning.

sections.title: Design investigations
sections.summary: Design investigations provide the information needed for adequate design and construction planning, reliably identify ground disposition/properties affecting the works, and establish performance-governing parameters before final design; particular geological features (cavities, degradation, faults, expansible/collapsible soils, waste) and ground-water levels must be established.
sections.body: Design investigations shall be carried out to provide the information required for an adequate design of the temporary and permanent works, to plan the method of construction, and to identify any difficulties that may arise during construction. The design investigation shall reliably identify the disposition and properties of all ground relevant to or affected by the proposed construction, and the parameters affecting the structure's ability to satisfy its performance criteria shall be established before the start of final design. Particular attention should be paid to ground profile, natural or man-made cavities, degradation of rocks/soils/fill, hydrogeological effects, faults/joints/discontinuities, creeping soil and rock masses, expansible and collapsible soils and rocks, and the presence of waste or man-made materials. Site and surroundings history shall be taken into account, investigation shall extend at least through the relevant formations, existing ground-water levels (and any free water levels observed) shall be established and recorded (EN 1997-2), extreme water levels of any influencing water source should be established, and the location/capacity of nearby dewatering or water-abstraction wells shall be established.
key_points: Provides data for design of temporary/permanent works and for planning construction method
Must reliably identify ground disposition/properties relevant to or affected by construction
Performance-governing parameters established before start of final design
Particular geological features requiring attention: cavities, degradation, faults, creep, expansible/collapsible ground, waste
Existing and extreme ground-water levels, and nearby dewatering/abstraction wells, must be established
sections.applicability: Main design-phase investigation providing the parameters used directly in the geotechnical design calculations.

sections.title: Evaluation of geotechnical parameters - General
sections.summary: Only the most commonly used laboratory and field tests are referenced in this clause; other tests may be used where their suitability has been demonstrated through comparable experience.
sections.body: In the requirements concerning evaluation of geotechnical parameters given in this Section, only the most commonly used laboratory and field tests are referred to. Other tests may be used provided their suitability has been demonstrated through comparable experience.
key_points: Only the most common lab/field tests are explicitly covered
Other test methods are permitted if their suitability is demonstrated by comparable experience
sections.applicability: Framing clause introducing the parameter-evaluation guidance of 3.3.

sections.title: Characterisation of soil and rock type
sections.summary: The character and basic constituents of soil or rock must be identified before other test results are interpreted, using a recognised classification/description system; soils are described via grain size, density, water content, Atterberg limits, etc., and rock via weathering, jointing (type/width/spacing/fill), mineralogy, and strength indices.
sections.body: The character and basic constituents of the soil or rock shall be identified before the results of other tests are interpreted; the material shall be examined, identified and described in accordance with a recognised nomenclature, and a geological evaluation made. Soils should be classified and described according to an acknowledged geotechnical soil classification system; rock should be classified in terms of the quality of the solid (stone) material (weathering, particle organisation, grain size, hardness/toughness) and jointing (type, width, spacing, fill quality). Classification/identification tests for soils may include grain size distribution, weight density, porosity, water content, grain shape and surface roughness, density index, Atterberg limits, swelling, carbonate content, and organic matter content; for rocks, mineralogy, petrography, water content, weight density, porosity, sound velocity, quick water absorption, swelling, slake-durability index, and uniaxial compressive strength.
key_points: Material character/constituents identified and classified before interpreting other tests
Soils classified per an acknowledged geotechnical classification system
Rock classified by stone-material quality and jointing characteristics
Lists typical soil classification tests (grain size, Atterberg limits, density index, etc.)
Lists typical rock classification tests (mineralogy, sound velocity, slake-durability, UCS, etc.)
sections.applicability: Baseline material characterisation preceding quantitative geotechnical parameter derivation.

sections.title: Weight density
sections.summary: Weight density shall be determined with sufficient accuracy for the actions derived from it, typically from undisturbed samples (EN 1997-2) or from well-established correlations, e.g. with penetration tests.
sections.body: The weight density shall be determined with sufficient accuracy to establish design or characteristic values of the actions that derive from it. It should be determined on specimens of soil and rock taken from undisturbed samples (EN 1997-2), or alternatively derived from well established or documented correlations based on, for example, penetration tests.
key_points: Weight density accuracy must support the actions derived from it
Preferred source is testing of undisturbed samples
Correlation-based estimates (e.g. from penetration tests) are an accepted alternative
sections.applicability: Determination of weight density for use in geotechnical action and stress calculations.

sections.title: Density index
sections.summary: The density index expresses the degree of compaction of a non-cohesive soil relative to its loosest and densest states, as defined by standard laboratory procedures.
sections.body: The density index shall express the degree of compaction of a non-cohesive soil with respect to the loosest and densest condition as defined by standard laboratory procedures.
key_points: Density index quantifies compaction state of non-cohesive soil
Referenced against standard laboratory loosest/densest states
sections.applicability: Characterisation of relative density for granular (non-cohesive) soils.

sections.title: Degree of compaction
sections.summary: The degree of compaction of natural ground or fill is expressed as the ratio between dry weight density and the maximum dry weight density from a standard compaction test.
sections.body: The degree of compaction of natural ground or fill shall be expressed as the ratio between dry weight density and maximum dry weight density obtained from a standard compaction test.
key_points: Degree of compaction = dry weight density / maximum dry weight density (standard compaction test)
sections.applicability: Quality control metric for compacted natural ground or engineered fill.

sections.title: Shear strength
sections.summary: Shear strength assessment must consider stress level, anisotropy (especially low-plasticity clays), fissuring (stiff clays), strain rate, large strains, pre-formed slip surfaces, time effects, sensitivity, and saturation; effective parameters c' and tan(phi') are valid only over the stress range they were evaluated for.
sections.body: In assessing the shear strength of soil, the influence of stress level, anisotropy of strength (especially in low-plasticity clays), fissures (especially in stiff clays), strain rate effects, very large strains, pre-formed slip surfaces, time effects, sensitivity of cohesive soil, and degree of saturation shall be considered. When strength assessment is based on test results, confidence in the derivation theory, sample disturbance, and sample heterogeneity should be taken into account; time effects depend on permeability, availability of free water, and problem geometry. The values of effective shear strength parameters c' and tan(phi') shall be assumed constant only within the range of stresses for which they have been evaluated.
key_points: Multiple factors affect shear strength assessment: stress level, anisotropy, fissuring, strain rate, time
Sample disturbance and heterogeneity affect confidence in test-derived strength
Undrained duration depends on permeability, free-water availability, and geometry
c' and tan(phi') are valid only over the stress range in which they were evaluated
sections.applicability: General principles for deriving and applying soil shear strength parameters (c', phi', cu).

sections.title: Soil stiffness
sections.summary: Soil stiffness assessment must consider drainage conditions, mean effective stress level, pre-consolidation, and imposed strain/stress level; laboratory measurements often underestimate in-situ stiffness due to sample disturbance, so observations of previous construction behaviour should be analysed where available.
sections.body: In assessing soil stiffness, the following features shall be considered: drainage conditions, level of mean effective stress, natural or artificial pre-consolidation, and level of imposed shear strain or induced shear stress (often normalised with respect to shear strength at failure). Reliable stiffness measurements are often difficult to obtain from field or laboratory tests; due to sample disturbance and other effects, laboratory measurements often underestimate the in-situ stiffness of the soil, so observations of the behaviour of previous constructions should be analysed wherever available.
key_points: Stiffness assessment factors: drainage, mean effective stress, pre-consolidation, strain/stress level
Laboratory stiffness measurements often underestimate true in-situ stiffness (sample disturbance)
Comparable-experience observations of prior construction behaviour should supplement testing
sections.applicability: General principles for deriving soil stiffness/deformation parameters for settlement analysis.

sections.title: Quality and properties of rocks and rock masses - General assessment
sections.summary: Rock assessment must distinguish intact-material behaviour (core samples) from rock-mass behaviour (governed by discontinuities: spacing, orientation, aperture, persistence, tightness, roughness, filling); in-situ stresses, water pressure, and inter-layer variation must also be considered, and rock mass classification (EN 1997-2) may estimate mass strength/stiffness/jointing/permeability/weathering-deformation properties.
sections.body: In assessing the quality and properties of rocks and rock masses, a distinction shall be drawn between the behaviour of rock material as measured on undisturbed core samples and the behaviour of much larger rock masses, which include structural discontinuities such as bedding planes, joints, shear zones and solution cavities; joint spacing, orientation, aperture, persistence, tightness, roughness, and filling shall be considered. In-situ stresses, water pressure, and pronounced property variation between layers shall also be considered where relevant. Rock mass classification (EN 1997-2) may be used to estimate strength/stiffness, jointing (especially in fractured zones), joint-system water permeability, and deformation properties of weathered rock. Sensitivity of rocks to climate or stress changes, and the influence of chemical degradation on rock foundation performance, shall be assessed; some porous soft rocks degrade rapidly to low-strength soils when weathered, some rocks exhibit high solution rates (channels, caverns, sinkholes), and some rocks swell markedly when unloaded and exposed to air due to clay-mineral water absorption.
key_points: Distinguish intact rock-material behaviour from rock-mass behaviour governed by discontinuities
Joint characteristics to assess: spacing, orientation, aperture, persistence, tightness, roughness, filling
Rock mass classification (EN 1997-2) estimates mass strength/stiffness/jointing/permeability/deformation
Assess sensitivity to climate/stress changes and chemical degradation
Watch for rapid weathering degradation, solution features, and swelling on unloading
sections.applicability: General framework for assessing rock and rock-mass quality ahead of parameter derivation.

sections.title: Uniaxial compressive strength and deformability of rock materials
sections.summary: Assessment of UCS and deformability of rock materials must consider loading-axis orientation relative to anisotropy/bedding/foliation, sampling/storage history, number and geometry of specimens tested, water content/saturation at test time, test duration/stress rate, and the method of determining Young's modulus.
sections.body: In assessing the uniaxial compressive strength and deformability of rock materials, the influence of the following shall be considered: orientation of the loading axis with respect to specimen anisotropy/bedding planes/foliation; method of sampling, storage history and environment; number of specimens tested; geometry of the tested specimens; water content and degree of saturation at time of test; test duration and stress rate; and the method for determination of Young's modulus and the axial stress level(s) at which it is determined.
key_points: Loading-axis orientation relative to rock anisotropy/bedding/foliation affects measured strength
Sampling/storage history, specimen count and geometry, saturation, and test rate all influence results
Young's modulus determination method and stress level must be documented
sections.applicability: Testing and interpretation guidance for intact rock strength and deformability parameters.

sections.title: Shear strength of joints
sections.summary: Joint shear strength assessment must consider joint orientation relative to the assumed action direction, shear-test orientation, specimen count/dimensions, pore-water pressure, and progressive failure; joints/bedding/schistosity/cleavage or soil-rock/concrete-rock interfaces are typically the governing weak planes for limit equilibrium analysis.
sections.body: In assessing the shear strength of joints of rock materials, the influence of the following shall be considered: orientation of the joint relative to the assumed direction of actions; orientation of the shear test; number of specimens tested; dimensions of the sheared area; pore-water pressure conditions; and the possibility of progressive failure governing rock-mass behaviour. Planes of weakness in rock normally coincide with joints, bedding, schistosity or cleavage planes, or with soil-rock or concrete-rock interfaces; shear-strength measurements on these planes should normally be used for limit equilibrium analysis of rock masses.
key_points: Joint orientation relative to loading direction is a key factor in joint shear strength assessment
Pore-water pressure and progressive failure potential must be considered
Weak planes (joints, bedding, cleavage, soil/concrete-rock interfaces) govern limit equilibrium analysis of rock masses
sections.applicability: Shear strength characterisation of rock discontinuities for stability analysis of rock masses.

sections.title: Permeability and consolidation parameters of soil
sections.summary: Assessment of soil permeability/consolidation parameters must consider heterogeneity, anisotropy, fissures/faults, and stress-change effects; in-situ tests measuring large ground volumes are preferred over small laboratory samples, with attention to permeability change under increased effective stress, and grain-size-based estimation is sometimes used.
sections.body: In assessing permeability and consolidation parameters, the effects of heterogeneity, anisotropy, fissures or faults, and stress changes under the proposed loading shall be considered. Permeability measurements on small laboratory samples may not represent in-situ conditions; in-situ tests measuring average properties of a large ground volume should therefore be preferred where possible, while considering possible permeability changes with increased effective stress above the in-situ value. Permeability may sometimes be evaluated from grain size distribution.
key_points: Heterogeneity, anisotropy, fissures/faults, and stress changes affect permeability/consolidation assessment
In-situ (large-volume) tests are preferred over small laboratory samples for permeability
Permeability may change with increased effective stress above the in-situ value
Grain size distribution can support permeability estimation
sections.applicability: Derivation of soil permeability and consolidation parameters for seepage/consolidation analysis.

sections.title: Permeability parameters of rock
sections.summary: Rock mass permeability, governed mainly by jointing/discontinuities, shall be measured by appropriate in-situ tests (e.g. pumping tests with flow logging and joint-pattern mapping) or evaluated from local experience; laboratory permeability tests are limited to studying discontinuity effects such as variable aperture.
sections.body: Since the permeability of rock masses depends mainly on the degree of jointing and the existence of other discontinuities such as fractures and fissures, it shall be measured by appropriate in-situ tests or evaluated from local experience. In-situ permeability may be determined by a system of pumping tests combined with flow logging, considering the spatial hydrogeological flow conditions around the structure and the mapping of joint/discontinuity patterns. Laboratory permeability tests should only be used to study discontinuity effects, e.g. in terms of variable aperture.
key_points: Rock mass permeability is governed mainly by jointing and discontinuities
In-situ pumping/flow-logging tests, combined with joint-pattern mapping, are the preferred method
Laboratory tests are limited to studying discontinuity-scale effects such as aperture variability
sections.applicability: Derivation of rock mass permeability parameters.

sections.title: Geotechnical parameters from field tests - Cone penetration test
sections.summary: CPT interpretation must account for cone/friction-sleeve design, the need for confirmatory borings to establish the soil layer succession, ground-water/overburden effects, selection of representative values in heterogeneous soils with fluctuating results, and correlations with other test/density results.
sections.body: In assessing values of cone resistance, sleeve friction, and possibly pore-water pressure during penetration, the following shall be taken into account: the detailed design of the cone and friction sleeve (which may significantly affect results); that results can only be interpreted with confidence once the soil layer succession is established, often requiring supporting borings; effects of ground-water and overburden; in heterogeneous soils with widely fluctuating results, selecting penetration values for the zone of soil relevant to the construction; and established correlations with other test results such as density measurements and other penetration tests.
key_points: Cone/friction-sleeve design affects results significantly; allowance must be made for cone type used
Confident interpretation generally requires supporting borings to establish soil layering
Ground-water and overburden effects, and value selection in heterogeneous/fluctuating profiles, must be handled carefully
Correlations with other tests (density, other penetration methods) support interpretation
sections.applicability: Interpretation guidance specific to cone penetration test (CPT/CPTU) results.

sections.title: Standard penetration and dynamic probing test
sections.summary: Blow-count assessment must consider test type and detailed procedure, ground-water conditions, overburden pressure influence, and ground nature (particularly cobbles/coarse gravel).
sections.body: In assessing blow counts from standard penetration or dynamic probing tests, the following features shall be considered: type of test; detailed description of the test procedure; ground-water conditions; the influence of overburden pressure; and the nature of the ground, particularly if cobbles or coarse gravel are encountered.
key_points: Test type and detailed procedure must be documented
Ground-water conditions and overburden pressure influence blow-count interpretation
Coarse ground (cobbles, coarse gravel) can distort results
sections.applicability: Interpretation guidance for SPT and dynamic probing test results.

sections.title: Vane test
sections.summary: Vane test assessment considers test procedure detail, whether standardised equipment was used, whether a multi-depth strength profile was obtained, and rod skin friction; the test estimates undrained shear strength (cu) of cohesive soil, with measured values corrected by an experience-based factor (e.g. liquid limit, plasticity index, effective vertical stress).
sections.body: In assessing vane test results the following shall be considered: details of the test procedure; whether standardised vane equipment was used; whether measurements were made at several depths to provide a strength profile through the soil layer succession; and skin friction along the rod. Vane tests may be used to assess the undrained shear strength (cu) of cohesive soil; a NOTE observes the vane test is a simple, cheap way of checking trafficability of soft ground for heavy equipment. Derived cu values should be corrected by a factor based on local experience, depending for example on liquid limit, plasticity index, and effective vertical stress.
key_points: Vane test procedure detail and equipment standardisation must be documented
Multi-depth measurements can provide an undrained strength profile
Vane test is used to assess undrained shear strength cu of cohesive soil
Derived cu values require an empirical correction factor based on local experience (e.g. liquid limit, PI, effective vertical stress)
sections.applicability: Interpretation guidance for field vane shear test results (undrained strength of cohesive soils).

sections.title: Weight sounding test
sections.summary: Weight sounding test assessment considers test procedure, ground-water conditions, overburden influence, and ground nature; the test is used to assess soil layer boundaries and the density of non-cohesive soils.
sections.body: In assessing weight sounding test results, the following shall be taken into account: detailed description of the test procedure; ground-water conditions; influence of overburden pressure; and nature of the ground, particularly if cobbles or coarse gravel are encountered. Weight sounding tests may be used for assessment of soil layer boundaries and the density of non-cohesive soils.
key_points: Same core considerations as other penetration tests: procedure, ground-water, overburden, coarse ground
Primary use: identifying soil layer boundaries and density of non-cohesive soils
sections.applicability: Interpretation guidance for weight sounding test results.

sections.title: Pressuremeter test
sections.summary: Assessment of limit pressure and pressuremeter modulus considers equipment type and installation procedure; disturbed test curves should be discarded, and where the limit pressure is not reached, conservative extrapolation (or correlation from partial curves) may be used.
sections.body: In assessing values of the limit pressure and pressuremeter modulus, the type of equipment and the procedure used to install the pressuremeter in the ground shall be taken into account. Test curves exhibiting more than a moderate degree of disturbance should not be used. Where the limit pressure is not reached during the test, a moderate and conservative extrapolation of the curve may be used to estimate it; for tests recording only the initial part of the curve, general or (preferably) local correlations from the same site may be used conservatively to estimate the limit pressure from the pressuremeter modulus.
key_points: Equipment type and installation procedure strongly affect pressuremeter results
Disturbed test curves should be discarded
Limit pressure may be conservatively extrapolated, or estimated via correlation, if not directly reached
sections.applicability: Interpretation guidance for pressuremeter test results, feeding Annex E bearing resistance estimation.

sections.title: Dilatometer test
sections.summary: Dilatometer value assessment must account for the installation procedure and pre-determined soil succession/granularity/saturation; penetration resistance informs strength parameter evaluation, and dilatometer values serve as an index for deriving soil stiffness moduli.
sections.body: In assessing dilatometer values, the installation procedure shall be taken into account, and the succession of soil layers and basic parameters such as granularity and degree of saturation shall be determined prior to the test. If strength parameters are to be evaluated, the penetration resistance should be taken into account. Dilatometer values should be used as an index for determining derived values of the stiffness moduli of the soil succession.
key_points: Installation procedure and pre-test knowledge of soil succession/granularity/saturation are important
Penetration resistance supports strength parameter evaluation
Primary application: index values for deriving soil stiffness moduli
sections.applicability: Interpretation guidance for flat dilatometer test (DMT) results.

sections.title: Compactibility tests
sections.summary: Fill compactibility assessment considers soil/rock type, grain size and shape, material heterogeneity, saturation/water content, and compaction plant type; field measurements used to control site compaction should be related to standard laboratory compaction values via field compaction trials (5.3.3(4)).
sections.body: In assessing the compactibility of a fill material, the following shall be taken into account: type of soil or rock; grain size distribution; grain shape; heterogeneity of the material; degree of saturation or water content; and type of plant to be used. When using field measurements (soundings, dynamic compaction tests, plate load tests, settlement records) to control site compaction, the results of field compaction trials (see 5.3.3(4)) should be related to standard laboratory compaction test values to assess compactibility of a soil or rock fill.
key_points: Compactibility depends on material type, grading, shape, heterogeneity, saturation, and compaction plant
Field compaction control measurements should be tied back to laboratory compaction test values via field trials
sections.applicability: Assessment framework for fill material compactibility, feeding Section 5 fill construction requirements.

sections.title: Ground Investigation Report - Requirements
sections.summary: Geotechnical investigation results are compiled in a Ground Investigation Report, forming part of the Geotechnical Design Report (2.8), referencing EN 1997-2 for lab/field test use; the report normally comprises a presentation of all available geotechnical information plus a geotechnical evaluation stating interpretation assumptions.
sections.body: The results of a geotechnical investigation shall be compiled in a Ground Investigation Report, which shall form part of the Geotechnical Design Report described in 2.8; reference shall be made to EN 1997-2 for the use of laboratory and field tests for geotechnical parameters. The Ground Investigation Report should normally consist of a presentation of all available geotechnical information (including geological features and relevant data) and a geotechnical evaluation of that information stating the assumptions made in interpreting the test results; the information may be presented as one report or as separate parts.
key_points: Ground Investigation Report is part of the overall Geotechnical Design Report
Comprises a factual presentation of geotechnical information plus a geotechnical evaluation
May be a single report or separate parts
sections.applicability: Documentation requirement linking site investigation results to the design process.

sections.title: Presentation of geotechnical information
sections.summary: The factual account must document all field/lab work and methods used (per EN 1997-2 test reports), and should additionally cover consultants/scope/dates, field reconnaissance findings, local experience, seismicity, sampling/storage procedures, equipment, tabulated quantities, ground-water fluctuation data, boring logs with photographs, and radon/frost-susceptibility notes.
sections.body: The presentation of geotechnical information shall include a factual account of all field and laboratory work, and documentation of the methods used to carry out the field investigations and laboratory testing, based on the test reports described in EN 1997-2. The factual account should additionally include, as relevant: names of consultants/subcontractors; purpose and scope of the investigation; dates of field/lab work; field reconnaissance findings (ground-water evidence, neighbouring structure behaviour, quarry/borrow exposures, instability areas, excavation difficulties, site history, geology including faulting, survey data, aerial photographs); local area experience; area seismicity information; sampling/transport/storage procedures; field equipment types used; tabulation of field/lab work quantities and field observations; ground-water table fluctuation data (boreholes and post-completion piezometers); compilation of boring logs with core photographs and descriptions; occurrence or possibility of radon; frost susceptibility data; and grouping/presentation of field and laboratory results in appendices.
key_points: Factual account of all field/lab work, documented per EN 1997-2 test report standards
Should cover scope, dates, personnel, and field reconnaissance observations
Should include ground-water fluctuation data and full boring log compilation with photographs
Should note radon occurrence potential and frost susceptibility data
sections.applicability: Content checklist for the factual (as opposed to interpretive) part of the Ground Investigation Report.

sections.title: Evaluation of geotechnical information
sections.summary: The evaluation must review field/lab work (flagging data limitations and considering sampling/storage/adverse results), review derived parameter values, and propose/justify any further investigation with a specific programme; it should also include tabulated/graphical presentation, histograms, ground-water depth/fluctuation, subsurface profiles, formation descriptions, irregularity notes, and value ranges/groupings per stratum.
sections.body: The evaluation of geotechnical information shall include a review of the field and laboratory work (pointing out and commenting on any data limitations such as defective, irrelevant, insufficient, or inaccurate data, considering sampling/transport/storage procedures, and carefully assessing any particularly adverse results to determine if they are misleading or represent a real phenomenon requiring design accommodation); a review of the derived values of geotechnical parameters; and any proposals for further field/laboratory work, justified and accompanied by a detailed programme addressing specific outstanding questions. As relevant, the evaluation should also include tabulation and graphical presentation of results against project requirements, histograms of the range/distribution of key data, ground-water table depth and seasonal fluctuation, subsurface profiles differentiating formations, detailed formation descriptions (physical, deformation, strength characteristics), comments on irregularities such as pockets and cavities, and the range/grouping of derived values for each stratum.
key_points: Requires a critical review of field/lab work data limitations and adverse results
Requires a review of derived geotechnical parameter values
Any proposed further investigation must be justified with a specific programme
Recommended supporting content: histograms, subsurface profiles, formation descriptions, per-stratum value ranges
sections.applicability: Content checklist for the interpretive/evaluation part of the Ground Investigation Report.
